blocks.title: Therapeutic index
blocks.text: The therapeutic index (TI) is a quantitative measure of a drug's safety. It compares the dose that causes a toxic effect with the dose that produces the desired therapeutic effect: TI = TD50 / ED50.

blocks.alt: Top: two S-shaped curves of patients responding against dose: efficacy (blue) rises first, with ED50 marked; toxicity (red) rises at higher doses, with TD50 marked; a green band between them is the therapeutic window, and TI = TD50/ED50. Bottom: the drug level in the blood rises after one dose and then falls; a red dashed line marks the MTC and a green dashed line the MEC; the band between them is the therapeutic window, and an arrow marks the duration of action while the level is above the MEC.
blocks.caption: Therapeutic window and therapeutic index (original diagram after Figure 32.1).
blocks.long_description: A drug helps when its level is above the MEC and harms when it rises above the MTC. The further apart the efficacy and toxicity curves are, the wider the window and the safer the drug.

items: TD50 (toxic dose 50) is the dose that causes a toxic effect in 50% of the people who take it.
ED50 (effective dose 50) is the dose that works for 50% of the people who take it.

blocks.text: A higher TI means the drug is safer, because there is a larger difference between the effective dose and the toxic dose; a low TI means the drug is more dangerous and needs careful monitoring. For example, a drug with a TI of 10 is much safer than one with a TI of 2. The book gives penicillin and paracetamol as drugs with a high TI, so an accidental double dose would not threaten the patient's life. Warfarin (a blood thinner) and digoxin (a heart medicine) have a low TI and must be taken very carefully in the proper dose, otherwise they may risk the patient's life. Patients using low-TI drugs need regular blood tests for therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM).

blocks.title: Doses still matter
blocks.text: A high TI does not make a drug harmless in large amounts. An overdose of paracetamol, for example, can seriously damage the liver, so the stated dose must always be followed.

blocks.title: Did you know?
blocks.text: Before modern blood-level monitoring, digoxin was a frequent cause of accidental hospital deaths. Its TI is so low that even minor interactions with common foods or other drugs could push patients into a lethal 'toxic zone'. Its toxicity causes ventricular fibrillation (a fatal heart rhythm) and 'yellow-tinted' vision (xanthopsia).

blocks.prompt: Drug X has an ED50 of 5 mg and a TD50 of 100 mg. Calculate its therapeutic index.
blocks.explanation: TI = TD50 / ED50 = 100 / 5 = 20, a fairly safe drug.

items: High TI (penicillin): safer; low TI (warfarin, digoxin): needs monitoring (TDM).
